opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key thing with both drone flight and walking is that the physics are relatively well understood, and in a sense the robot is mostly dealing with itself. With a drone, you're controlling your own body moving through air. The aerodynamics can get complicated, but we have good models, and the drone can sense its own state very precisely with gyroscopes, accelerometers, and so on. With walking, it's similar. The robot is mainly controlling its own body, its joints and its balance, and the interaction with the world is fairly limited. It's your feet hitting the ground.

That matters because it means you can build quite accurate simulations. That's been the big breakthrough over the last several years. You can take a quadruped or a humanoid, put it in a simulator, and run millions of trials in parallel, essentially years of experience compressed into hours. Then you transfer that policy to the real robot, and with some randomization of parameters like friction and mass, it works remarkably well. That's why we're seeing all these videos of robots doing backflips, dancing, and running up hills. It's genuinely impressive, but it's impressive in a domain where simulation is a good proxy for reality.

The other thing is that these tasks are fairly forgiving. If your foot lands a centimeter off, you adjust on the next step. Walking is a continuous feedback loop where small errors get corrected. A drone that drifts a little just corrects its thrust.

Contrast that with manipulation: picking up an arbitrary object, folding a towel, or tying a knot. Now you're interacting with an object whose properties you don't know: its mass distribution, its friction, whether it's deformable. Contact mechanics are notoriously hard to simulate. Tiny differences at the micron level, in how surfaces touch, can determine whether an object slides out of your grasp or not. You can't see those properties with a camera, and they're very hard to model. So the sim-to-real gap is much larger, and small errors aren't forgiving. You drop the glass.

So I'd say the answer is that drone flight and walking are mostly about controlling yourself in a fairly predictable environment, which we can simulate. Manipulation is about controlling *other things* whose physics are uncertain. That's a big part of why people overestimate how close we are to general-purpose robots. They see the locomotion results and assume manipulation will follow just as quickly. I don't think it will.

r001.rationale: The response describes drones as controlling their own body and having precise state sensing, but it does not identify lower state-space dimensionality as the reason tolerable flight performance is easier.

r002.rationale: It says a drone that drifts a little can correct its thrust, clearly explaining that small position deviations are readily recoverable.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the key thing is the nature of the environment and what happens when you make a mistake. With a drone, you're flying through air. Air is pretty forgiving. You have a few state variables — position, orientation, velocity — and the dynamics are well understood. If you're a little bit off, you just correct. There's not a lot of complex contact going on. And the same is true for walking, in a sense. Walking looks hard, and it took a long time to get right, but there's a well-defined objective: stay upright, keep moving forward. Your feet touch the ground, but the ground is largely a known quantity. Legged robots like the Boston Dynamics ones have become remarkably good because the problem is relatively constrained and you can learn it in simulation very effectively, because the physics of walking transfers pretty well from sim to reality.

Now contrast that with manipulation. When you reach out to grasp something, you're dealing with contact. And contact is where everything gets ugly. Friction, deformation, the exact shape of the object, where your fingers land — small errors get amplified. If you're off by a few millimeters in grasping a glass, you might knock it over or miss it entirely. There's a huge amount of uncertainty, and that uncertainty doesn't wash out the way it does in flight. Plus the variety of objects is essentially infinite. Every kitchen, every warehouse has different things in it. So the space of what you have to be robust to is vastly larger.

I sometimes describe this as the difference between tasks where "good enough" is a wide target and tasks where it's a narrow one. For a drone, a tolerable trajectory is a big tube through the sky. For walking, there's a basin of stable gaits you can fall into. But for picking up an egg or threading a cable or folding a shirt, the window of acceptable actions is very tight, and perception has to be very good to even know where that window is. That's why I keep saying the hard part of robotics is not the body — it's the hands and what they touch.

r001.rationale: It says drone flight has “a few state variables” and links that constrained, well-understood problem to forgiving performance.

r002.rationale: It explains that if a drone is “a little bit off,” it can “just correct,” directly describing recovery from small deviations.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it is that you can keep correcting as you go. A drone doesn’t have to follow a perfectly precise trajectory to stay in the air. You can measure how it’s moving and make lots of small adjustments. And with walking, you don’t have to put your foot in exactly the same place every time. There’s a range of placements that will work, and you can adjust the next step.

Manipulation often gives you much less room for error. If you’re putting a peg into a hole, being a little bit off can mean it simply won’t go in. And when you make contact, the forces can change abruptly. So there’s a difference between getting roughly the right motion and actually completing the task. With flight and walking, that ability to tolerate deviations and continually correct them makes a big difference.

r001.rationale: The response discusses continual corrections in drone flight but does not identify lower state-space dimensionality as a reason tolerable performance is easier.

r002.rationale: It says a drone can measure its motion and make many small adjustments, communicating that it can recover from deviations in position or trajectory.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big part of it is that the environment gives you some room for error. With a drone, if you’re a few centimeters away from the trajectory you intended, that’s often fine, provided you’re not close to an obstacle. And with walking, you don’t have to put your foot in exactly the same place every time. You need to stay balanced and keep moving, but there’s a range of motions that will work.

Manipulation can be much less forgiving. If you’re trying to insert a connector, being a few millimeters off can mean it simply doesn’t go in. And when you make contact, the forces can change very quickly. So getting something to work tolerably well depends a lot on how much error the task allows, and whether you can recover from that error.

r001.rationale: The response says drones can tolerate small trajectory deviations, but does not attribute this to lower state-space dimensionality.

r002.rationale: It notes that small drone deviations are often fine, but does not explain this in terms of drones readily recovering from them.
